chapitres.resume: Axe 1, Identités et échanges : l'immigration au Canada, la Windrush generation au Royaume-Uni, la frontière irlandaise. Grammaire : choisir un temps du passé, le past perfect, les marqueurs temporels, used to / would et le futur dans le passé.
chapitres.chapeau: Millions of people have left their country to start a new life in Canada, in Britain or elsewhere. Their arrival changed their new homes, and their new homes changed them. Borders can separate people, but they can also be places where identities meet. Dans ce chapitre, tu lis trois histoires de migrations et de frontières, et tu apprends à raconter un parcours au passé en situant précisément les événements les uns par rapport aux autres.
objectifs: présenter la politique d'immigration du Canada, de Pier 21 au multiculturalisme ;
raconter l'histoire de la Windrush generation et expliquer le scandale de 2018 ;
expliquer pourquoi la frontière entre l'Irlande et l'Irlande du Nord est un enjeu d'identité ;

sections.html:
Le Canada se présente souvent comme un pays d'accueil. Lis le texte et repère trois étapes de sa politique d'immigration, puis ses zones d'ombre.

Pier 21

Between 1928 and 1971, about one million immigrants arrived in Canada through Pier 21, in the port of Halifax, Nova Scotia. After a long voyage across the Atlantic, they showed their papers, had a medical check and took a train to their new life. Today the building is the Canadian Museum of Immigration.

From origin to skills

For a long time, Canada chose its immigrants according to their country of origin and preferred Europeans. In 1967, the government introduced a points system: candidates now received points for their education, their knowledge of English or French and their work experience, not for their nationality. Skilled workers from Asia, Africa and the Caribbean could now be eligible.

In 1971, Prime Minister Pierre Elliott Trudeau announced a policy of multiculturalism: newcomers did not have to give up their culture to become Canadian. Canada was the first country in the world to adopt such a policy, and the Canadian Multiculturalism Act followed in 1988.

Canada today

According to the 2021 census, almost one Canadian in four (23 %) is or has been an immigrant. Newcomers arrive as skilled workers, through family sponsorship (a relative who already lives in Canada supports their application) or as refugees. Since 1979, groups of ordinary citizens have also been able to sponsor refugees privately: between November 2015 and February 2016, Canada welcomed more than 25,000 Syrian refugees.

A darker past

This open image has its shadows. From 1885, Chinese immigrants had to pay a head tax to enter the country, and a law excluded almost all of them from 1923 to 1947. In 1914, the ship Komagata Maru, carrying 376 passengers, most of them Sikhs from India, was turned away from Vancouver. The Canadian government apologised for the head tax in 2006 and for the Komagata Maru in 2016.

Méthode

Pour résumer un texte historique, relève les dates et associe chacune à un changement : 1967 → points system, 1971 → multiculturalism. Une frise chronologique (timeline) t'aide à restituer l'ordre des événements à l'oral.

En 1948, un navire arrive des Caraïbes en Angleterre. Ses passagers donnent leur nom à toute une génération. Lis le texte et repère ce que ces migrants ont apporté au Royaume-Uni, et comment ils ont été traités.

22 June 1948

On 22 June 1948, the ship HMT Empire Windrush arrived at Tilbury Docks, near London. On board were more than a thousand passengers, most of them from Jamaica, Trinidad and other Caribbean islands, which were British colonies at the time. Among them was the calypso singer Lord Kitchener, who sang London Is the Place for Me for the cameras.

That same year, the British Nationality Act made people from the colonies "citizens of the United Kingdom and Colonies": they had the right to live and work in Britain. The country needed them. After the Second World War, Britain had to rebuild its cities, and the new National Health Service (NHS), London Transport and the railways were looking for workers.

A lasting contribution

The people who came from the Caribbean between 1948 and 1971 are known as the Windrush generation. They worked as nurses, bus drivers, factory workers and engineers. Their culture changed British society: calypso, reggae, Caribbean food, and the Notting Hill Carnival, which has been held in London every August since 1966.

Life was not easy. Many landlords put up signs saying "No Irish, no Blacks, no dogs", and in 1958 white gangs attacked Caribbean residents during the Notting Hill riots. Yet the newcomers stayed, built communities and became part of the nation. One of the passengers, Sam King, became the first Black mayor of the London borough of Southwark in 1983.

The Windrush scandal

In 2018, the public discovered that hundreds of people from the Windrush generation had been wrongly treated as illegal immigrants. They had arrived legally as children, but they had never needed papers to prove it. The Home Office had even destroyed their landing cards in 2010. Some lost their jobs or their homes, some were refused healthcare, and some were sent to detention centres or deported. The Home Secretary, Amber Rudd, resigned, and the government created a compensation scheme. Since 2018, Windrush Day has celebrated the contribution of Caribbean migrants every year on 22 June.

L'île d'Irlande est partagée entre deux États. Lis le texte et repère comment cette frontière a d'abord séparé, puis rapproché, les habitants de l'île.

One island, two states

In 1921, Ireland was divided. Twenty-six counties became the Irish Free State in 1922, which later became the Republic of Ireland, while six counties in the north-east remained part of the United Kingdom as Northern Ireland. The border between them is about 500 kilometres long and crosses fields, villages and even farms.

In Northern Ireland, two communities lived side by side. Most unionists, mainly Protestants, wanted to stay British. Most nationalists, mainly Catholics, wished to join the Republic. Even the name of the second city depends on who you are talking to: Derry for many nationalists, Londonderry for many unionists.

The Troubles

From the late 1960s to 1998, a violent conflict known as the Troubles killed more than 3,500 people. During those years, the border was guarded by soldiers, with armed checkpoints and watchtowers, and many small roads were closed.

Peace and an open border

On 10 April 1998, the Good Friday Agreement brought peace. It recognised that the people of Northern Ireland may identify as British, Irish or both, and hold a British passport, an Irish passport or both. The checkpoints disappeared, and today you can cross the border without noticing it: people go to school, work or shop on the other side every day.

After Brexit

When the United Kingdom left the European Union in 2020, the open border became a problem, because it was now a border between the EU and a non-EU country. To avoid a "hard border" with checkpoints, London and Brussels agreed to carry out checks on some goods travelling between Great Britain and Northern Ireland, in the Irish Sea; the Windsor Framework of 2023 adjusted this arrangement. In Belfast, some "peace walls" still separate the two communities: the border question is also a question of identity.

Définition

Une frontière dure (hard border) comporte des postes de contrôle physiques ; une frontière ouverte (open border) se franchit librement. Le Royaume-Uni et l'Irlande forment depuis 1923 une zone de libre circulation, la Common Travel Area.

Pour raconter un parcours, il faut choisir le bon temps. Le choix dépend de la manière dont tu regardes l'action, pas seulement de sa date.

Le prétérit simple : une action terminée, datée

Il présente un fait passé, coupé du présent, souvent avec un repère daté (in 1948, ago, last year, when) : The Windrush arrived in 1948. Trudeau announced the policy in 1971.

Verbes irréguliers fréquents : come → came, leave → left, bring → brought, take → took, become → became, build → built, give → gave, lose → lost, choose → chose, send → sent.

Le prétérit be + -ing : une action en cours dans le passé

Il décrit une action en déroulement à un moment passé, souvent interrompue par une action au prétérit simple : The passengers were waiting on the deck when the ship arrived. Il sert aussi à poser un décor : It was raining and people were cheering.

When introduit souvent l'action courte (prétérit simple), while l'action longue (be + -ing) : While she was working at the hospital, she met her husband.

Le present perfect : un lien entre passé et présent

Il s'emploie quand le passé a un lien avec le présent : un bilan, une conséquence, une durée qui continue. On ne peut pas l'employer avec un repère daté et terminé.

  • bilan : Canada has welcomed millions of immigrants.
  • durée jusqu'à maintenant avec for (durée) et since (point de départ) : The carnival has been held since 1966. She has lived in Toronto for ten years.
  • avec already, ever, never, yet, just : Have you ever been to Halifax?
PhraseTempsPourquoi
She came to London in 1956.prétérit simpledate passée terminée
She has lived in London since 1956.present perfectelle y vit toujours
She was living in London when she met him.prétérit be + -ingaction en cours, interrompue
Attention

« Elle vit à Londres depuis 1956 » se dit She has lived in London since 1956 et non She lives in London since 1956. Et « il est arrivé il y a dix ans » se dit He arrived ten years ago (prétérit, jamais de present perfect avec ago).

Forme

had + participe passé, à toutes les personnes : I had left, she had arrived, they had never needed. Négation : had not (hadn't) + participe passé. Question : Had they arrived?

Emploi : le passé du passé

Le past perfect exprime une action antérieure à un autre moment du passé. Il correspond souvent au plus-que-parfait français (« ils étaient arrivés »).

  • In 2018, they discovered that the Home Office had destroyed the landing cards. (la destruction a eu lieu avant la découverte)
  • When the ship docked, the passengers had already spent three weeks at sea.
  • By the time the Troubles ended, more than 3,500 people had died.

Compare :

  • When I arrived, the train left. : j'arrive, puis le train part (succession).
  • When I arrived, the train had left. : le train était déjà parti (antériorité).

Les repères qui l'accompagnent souvent

already, just, never… before, by the time, after, before, when, until : She had never seen snow before she landed in Halifax.

Le past perfect be + -ing

had been + V-ing insiste sur la durée d'une activité jusqu'à un moment passé : They had been living in Britain for fifty years when they were told to leave.

Attention

On n'emploie pas le past perfect quand l'ordre des actions est évident et suit l'ordre du récit : She got off the ship, took a train and found a room. Le past perfect sert à revenir en arrière dans le temps.

sections.titre: Grammar: time markers, used to, would, was going to
sections.html:
Situer dans le temps

RelationMarqueursExemple
antérioritébefore, by the time, until, earlierBy the time she retired, she had worked for the NHS for 40 years.
simultanéitéwhile, as, when, in the meantime, meanwhileWhile the soldiers watched the border, smugglers used small roads.
postérioritéafter, as soon as, once, afterwards, later, the following yearAs soon as the ship docked, journalists rushed on board.
duréefor, since, over the past years, during, in a couple of daysOver the past years, immigration has increased.

Après when, as soon as, once, until, before, after à valeur future, on emploie le présent (et non will) : I'll call you as soon as I arrive.

L'habitude dans le passé : used to et would

  • used to + BV : une habitude ou un état passé qui n'existe plus : Soldiers used to check every car. There used to be a watchtower here. Négation : didn't use to ; question : Did you use to…?
  • would + BV : une action répétée dans le passé, souvent dans un récit de souvenirs : Every Sunday, my grandmother would cook rice and peas. Would ne s'emploie pas pour un état : She used to live in Kingston (pas would live).
Ne confonds pas

I used to work at night (j'avais l'habitude, ce n'est plus le cas) ; I am used to working at night (je suis habitué à) ; I got used to working at night (je me suis habitué à). Après be used to et get used to, to est une préposition : on emploie V-ing.

Le futur dans le passé

Pour parler, dans un récit au passé, de ce qui était alors à venir :

  • was / were going to + BV : une intention passée, souvent non réalisée : Many passengers were going to stay for five years, but they never went back.
  • would + BV : ce qui allait arriver, vu depuis le passé : In 1948, nobody knew that the ship would give its name to a generation.

chapitres.a_retenir:
• Le Canada a ouvert son immigration avec le système à points (1967) et la politique du multiculturalisme (1971) ; près d'un Canadien sur quatre est immigré (recensement de 2021). Son passé comporte aussi des exclusions (taxe d'entrée imposée aux Chinois, Komagata Maru).
  • La Windrush generation désigne les migrants venus des Caraïbes entre 1948 et 1971 pour aider à reconstruire le Royaume-Uni ; en 2018, le Windrush scandal a révélé que beaucoup avaient été traités à tort comme des clandestins.
  • La frontière irlandaise date de 1921 ; l'accord du Vendredi saint (1998) a mis fin aux Troubles et permet d'être britannique, irlandais ou les deux. Le Brexit a reposé la question de la frontière.
  • Prétérit simple : fait daté et terminé. Prétérit be + -ing : action en cours dans le passé. Present perfect : lien avec le présent (bilan, for, since), jamais avec ago ni une date terminée.
  • Past perfect (had + participe passé) : action antérieure à un autre moment du passé.
  • used to + BV : habitude ou état passé révolu ; would + BV : action répétée dans un souvenir ; was going to / would : futur vu depuis le passé.

sections.titre: Where you live, who you are?
sections.html:
Le lieu où l'on vit détermine l'accès à l'école, à l'emploi, aux transports. Lis le texte et repère comment des politiques publiques ont favorisé la ségrégation, puis tenté de la combattre.

Redlining in the United States

In the 1930s, during the Great Depression, a federal agency, the Home Owners' Loan Corporation, drew maps of American cities. Each neighbourhood received a grade from A to D. The "hazardous" D areas were coloured in red, and they were very often the neighbourhoods where Black families and immigrants lived. Banks then refused to lend money to people in those areas, or charged them more. This practice is called redlining.

Redlining denied millions of families access to homeownership, the main way to build wealth in the United States. It was banned by the Fair Housing Act, signed by President Lyndon B. Johnson in April 1968, a week after the assassination of Martin Luther King. Yet its effects can still be seen today: many formerly redlined neighbourhoods have higher poverty rates and fewer trees and parks.

Gated communities

Today, some wealthy Americans live in gated communities, residential areas surrounded by walls, with guards at the entrance. Residents say they feel safer; critics say these areas separate "the haves and the have-nots" and weaken the sense of a shared city.

Social housing in Britain

In the United Kingdom, local councils built millions of council houses after the Second World War, so that working families could rent a decent home. From 1980, the Right to Buy allowed tenants to buy their council homes, but few new ones were built. Today, many cities try to build mixed-tenure neighbourhoods, where private homes and social housing stand side by side. The fire at Grenfell Tower, a social housing block in one of the richest areas of London, killed 72 people in June 2017 and became a symbol of the gap between rich and poor residents.

sections.titre: The Supreme Court: inclusion and exclusion
sections.html:
Aux États-Unis, la Cour suprême dit si les lois respectent la Constitution. Ses décisions ont tantôt exclu, tantôt inclus les minorités. Lis le texte et classe les arrêts cités en deux colonnes : exclusion et inclusion.

How the Court works

The Supreme Court is the highest court in the United States. It is made up of nine Justices, led by the Chief Justice. They are nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate, and they serve for life. When a Justice dies or retires, the President can fill the vacancy, which is why each nomination is a major political battle. The Court decides by majority; a Justice who disagrees with the majority can write a dissenting opinion.

From exclusion…

In Plessy v. Ferguson (1896), the Court ruled that racial segregation was legal as long as facilities were "separate but equal". In practice, schools, trains and hospitals for Black Americans were separate, but far from equal. This decision protected segregation in the South for more than half a century.

… to inclusion

In Brown v. Board of Education (1954), the Court, led by Chief Justice Earl Warren, ruled unanimously that segregated public schools were unconstitutional. The lawyer who won the case, Thurgood Marshall, became the first Black Justice in 1967. Other decisions followed: Loving v. Virginia (1967) allowed interracial marriage in every state, and Obergefell v. Hodges (2015) did the same for same-sex marriage.

A court that can change its mind

The Court can also overturn its own precedents. In 2022, it overturned Roe v. Wade (1973), which had protected the right to abortion: each state can now decide. In 2023, it ruled that universities could no longer take race into account in their admissions, ending the use of affirmative action in college admissions. For some, these decisions protect the Constitution; for others, they wipe out rights that minorities had won.

Des juges qui ont marqué l'histoire

Ruth Bader Ginsburg, deuxième femme nommée à la Cour (1993-2020), célèbre pour ses opinions dissidentes ; Sonia Sotomayor, première juge d'origine hispanique (2009) ; Ketanji Brown Jackson, première femme noire (2022).

Comment les Peuples premiers (First Peoples, Indigenous peoples) peuvent-ils faire entendre leur voix dans les institutions ? Lis le texte et compare deux réponses, en Nouvelle-Zélande et en Australie.

New Zealand: Māori seats

In 1840, the British Crown and more than 500 Māori chiefs signed the Treaty of Waitangi, which is considered the founding document of New Zealand. In 1867, Parliament created four Māori seats, elected only by Māori voters, and gave the vote to all Māori men. There are now seven Māori electorates, and Māori MPs also sit for ordinary constituencies. Te reo Māori has been an official language since 1987.

Australia: the Voice referendum

In Australia, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples were long excluded. In the 1967 referendum, more than 90 % of voters agreed that they should be counted in the national census and that the federal government could make laws for them. In 2023, Australians were asked whether an Indigenous Voice to Parliament, an advisory body, should be written into the Constitution. On 14 October 2023, about 60 % voted no, and the proposal was rejected in every state.

Integration or appropriation?

Reserved seats and advisory bodies divide opinion. Supporters say they guarantee that First Peoples are heard and help to right historical wrongs. Critics answer that they can be symbolic only, giving recognition without real power, or that the majority uses Indigenous culture and symbols without sharing decisions. Others, on the contrary, reject any separate representation in the name of equality.

In the United States, Native Americans became citizens of the country in 1924. In 2021, Deb Haaland, a member of the Laguna Pueblo, became the first Native American to serve as a cabinet secretary.

Méthode : nuancer son accord

I partly agree with this idea, but… / That's a valid point; however… / I see what you mean, yet I differ from you on… / Let's agree to disagree.

Quand l'employer ?

  • quand l'agent est inconnu, évident ou sans importance : The Fair Housing Act was signed in 1968.
  • pour mettre en valeur ce qui subit l'action : Thousands of families were denied loans.
  • dans les textes officiels, juridiques et journalistiques.

Le passif des verbes à deux compléments

Avec give, offer, grant, tell, deny, la personne devient souvent le sujet : They gave Māori men the vote. → Māori men were given the vote. C'est l'équivalent de « on » en français : On leur a refusé un prêt = They were refused a loan.

Be said to, be thought to

He is said to be the best lawyer in the state : on dit qu'il est… The Treaty is considered (to be) the founding document of New Zealand.

Attention

Les verbes intransitifs (arrive, happen, die) n'ont pas de passif. Et le « on » français ne se traduit pas toujours par le passif : On dit que… = People say that… ou It is said that…

Une proposition relative apporte une information sur un nom (l'antécédent). Le pronom relatif dépend de l'antécédent et de sa fonction.

PronomAntécédentExemple
whopersonne, sujet (ou complément à l'oral)the lawyer who won the case
whompersonne, complément (registre soutenu), après prépositionthe Justice whom the President nominated / the chiefs with whom the Crown signed the treaty
whichchose, animalthe decision which ended segregation
thatpersonne ou chose, relative déterminative seulementthe law that banned redlining
whoseappartenance (« dont le / la / les »)families whose homes were redlined
where / whenlieu / momentthe area where she grew up / the year when the Act was signed

Whose

Whose est suivi directement du nom possédé, sans article : Ruth Bader Ginsburg, whose dissents became famous, served for 27 years. (dont les opinions dissidentes)

Relatives déterminatives et appositives

  • Déterminative (defining) : indispensable pour identifier l'antécédent, sans virgule ; that est possible : The Justices who wrote the opinion were in the majority.
  • Appositive (non-defining) : information supplémentaire, entre virgules ; that est impossible : Thurgood Marshall, who won Brown, joined the Court in 1967.

L'omission du relatif

Dans une déterminative, le relatif complément peut disparaître : the case (that) Marshall won, the woman (who) I met. Le relatif sujet ne peut pas être omis : the man who lives here.

Avec une préposition, l'anglais courant la rejette à la fin : the area (that) she lives in ; l'anglais soutenu dit the area in which she lives.

Attention

« Ce que » se dit what : What the Court decided surprised everyone. Et pour reprendre toute une proposition, on emploie which après une virgule : The proposal was rejected, which disappointed its supporters.

Vouloir que quelqu'un fasse

Le français emploie « que » + subjonctif ; l'anglais emploie verbe + complément + to + BV :

  • The activists want the government to build more social housing. (veulent que le gouvernement construise)
  • Voters expected the Court to protect their rights. (s'attendaient à ce que la Cour protège)
  • I would like you to explain your point of view. (j'aimerais que tu expliques)

Le complément est un pronom complément : She wants them to vote (jamais she wants that they vote).

D'autres verbes suivent ce modèle : ask, tell, allow, encourage, force, help, need, persuade, advise : The law allowed tenants to buy their homes. The judge told the parties to stand up. Négation : not avant to : She asked them not to leave.

Make, let et be made to

make (obliger) et let (laisser) sont suivis de la base verbale sans to : The guards made visitors show their ID. They let us in. Au passif, to réapparaît : Visitors were made to show their ID.

Empêcher, interdire

prevent / stop / bar + sb + from + V-ing : Redlining prevented families from buying homes. They were barred from voting.

Attention

Hope ne suit pas ce modèle : I hope (that) they will win, et non I hope them to win. Avec suggest, on dit I suggest that she (should) apply ou I suggest applying.

chapitres.a_retenir:
• Le redlining (années 1930) a privé des quartiers noirs et immigrés de prêts immobiliers ; le Fair Housing Act (1968) l'a interdit. Au Royaume-Uni, les council houses et les quartiers mixtes visent la mixité sociale.
  • La Cour suprême compte neuf juges nommés à vie par le président et confirmés par le Sénat. Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) a validé la ségrégation ; Brown v. Board of Education (1954) l'a déclarée inconstitutionnelle à l'école. La Cour peut renverser ses précédents (Roe v. Wade en 2022).

  • Passif : be + participe passé ; be porte le temps ; agent introduit par by ; « on » se traduit souvent par un passif (They were given the vote).

chapitres.chapeau: Kings and presidents have always used painters to show their power. But artists can also mock the powerful, denounce injustice or give a face to those who are ignored. Dans ce chapitre, tu étudies des portraits officiels, des œuvres engagées, des caricatures et des photographies de presse, et tu apprends à rapporter les paroles d'un artiste, à poser des questions indirectes et à insister sur une idée.

sections.html:
Un portrait officiel n'est pas une simple ressemblance : c'est un message politique. Lis le texte et repère, pour chaque œuvre, les éléments qui expriment le pouvoir.

The Armada Portrait

Queen Elizabeth I, who reigned over England from 1558 to 1603, carefully controlled her image. In the famous Armada Portrait, painted around 1588, she stands in a richly decorated dress covered with pearls, a symbol of purity. In the background, two windows show the Spanish Armada, the fleet that had tried to invade England: on one side the ships are sailing, on the other they are wrecked in a storm. Her right hand rests on a globe, as if England could now rule the seas. As she grew older, painters were expected to show her with a young, ageless face.

The Obama portraits

In 2018, the National Portrait Gallery in Washington, D.C. unveiled the official portraits of Barack and Michelle Obama. They were painted by Kehinde Wiley and Amy Sherald, the first Black artists chosen by the gallery for an official presidential portrait. Wiley shows the former president seated in front of a wall of leaves and flowers that represent Chicago, Hawaii and Kenya, the places that shaped his life. Sherald painted the former First Lady in grey tones, wearing a long geometric dress. For many visitors, seeing these portraits in a national museum was a form of recognition.

Public patronage

Power does not only commission portraits. During the Great Depression, the US government launched the Federal Art Project (1935-1943), part of President Franklin D. Roosevelt's New Deal. It employed thousands of unemployed artists, who painted murals in post offices, schools and hospitals. Art became a public service, but it also conveyed the government's optimistic message about work and the nation.

Méthode : décrire une image

Situe les éléments : in the foreground / in the background, in the middle, on the left / on the right, in the top left-hand corner, at the bottom. Puis interprète : This detail suggests that… / It is symbolic of… / The artist wants to convey the idea that…

L'art peut témoigner, dénoncer, ou rendre visibles ceux que l'histoire oubliait. Lis le texte et dis, pour chaque œuvre, si elle relève plutôt de la résistance ou de la reconnaissance.

Telling a forgotten story

Between 1940 and 1941, the young African American painter Jacob Lawrence created The Migration Series, sixty small panels telling the story of the Great Migration: the departure of millions of Black Americans from the rural South to the industrial cities of the North, where they hoped to escape segregation and find work. With simple shapes and bright colours, Lawrence turned the experience of ordinary people into history painting.

Denouncing injustice

In 1939, the jazz singer Billie Holiday recorded Strange Fruit, a song based on a poem by Abel Meeropol. Its "strange fruit" are the bodies of Black men lynched and hanging from trees in the South. Many radio stations refused to play it, but the song became one of the first great protest songs of the civil rights era.

In 1964, the illustrator Norman Rockwell, famous for his cheerful magazine covers, painted The Problem We All Live With. It shows Ruby Bridges, a six-year-old Black girl, walking to a newly desegregated school in New Orleans in 1960, escorted by four US marshals. On the wall behind her, we can read a racist insult and see the stain of a thrown tomato. The painting exposed the violence of segregation to millions of white readers.

Recognition and repair

Art also raises the question of who owns the past. In 1897, British soldiers looted thousands of objects, now known as the Benin Bronzes, from the Kingdom of Benin, in present-day Nigeria. For more than a century they were displayed in Western museums. Today, some institutions have begun to repatriate them: in 2022, the Horniman Museum in London transferred ownership of 72 objects to Nigeria. For many, returning looted artefacts is a way to come to terms with colonial history.

Dans la presse, un dessin ou une photographie peut avoir plus d'effet qu'un long article. Lis le texte et repère ce que chaque artiste voulait dénoncer.

From Hogarth to Punch

In 1751, the London artist William Hogarth published two prints, Beer Street and Gin Lane. In Beer Street, people are healthy and hard-working; in Gin Lane, cheap gin has destroyed everything: a drunk mother lets her baby fall, houses are collapsing. The prints supported a law to reduce gin drinking.

Fifty years later, James Gillray mocked the most powerful men of his time, including King George III and Napoleon. In The Plumb-pudding in Danger (1805), the British Prime Minister William Pitt and Napoleon are cutting the globe like a Christmas pudding to share the world between them. In 1841, the satirical magazine Punch was founded in London; it was Punch that first used the word "cartoon" for a humorous drawing, in 1843.

Photographs that testify

In 1936, during the Great Depression, Dorothea Lange photographed a poor mother and her children in a camp of farm workers in California. Migrant Mother became the symbol of the crisis and encouraged the government to send help.

In 1942, Gordon Parks, who later became the first Black staff photographer of Life magazine, photographed Ella Watson, a cleaning woman, standing with a mop and a broom in front of the American flag. He called the picture American Gothic, Washington, D.C., a reference to a famous painting, to show that the American dream was not open to everyone.

In South Africa, Peter Magubane photographed the apartheid regime for decades, including the Soweto uprising of 1976. He was arrested several times and spent long periods in prison, but he never stopped documenting injustice.

Définition

Le photojournalisme (photojournalism) raconte l'actualité par l'image ; la caricature (caricature, cartoon) exagère les traits d'une personne pour la critiquer ou s'en moquer.

Faux amis

A cartoon = un dessin humoristique ou un dessin animé (un carton = a cardboard box). A figure peut désigner une silhouette ou un personnage dans une œuvre (le visage = the face).

Say, tell, ask

  • say (that) : sans complément de personne : He said (that) photography was his weapon. Si l'on veut nommer l'interlocuteur : say to sb.
  • tell sb (that) : toujours suivi de la personne : She told the journalist (that) she was proud. (jamais she told that)
  • ask : pour une question ou une demande : He asked me to wait. She asked if I liked the portrait.

Autres verbes introducteurs utiles : explain, claim, admit, deny, add, answer, reply, warn, promise, suggest.

La concordance des temps

Quand le verbe introducteur est au passé, les temps reculent d'un cran :

Discours directDiscours rapporté
present simple : "I paint people."preterite : He said he painted people.
present be + -ing : "I am working."preterite be + -ing : She said she was working.
preterite / present perfect : "I saw it." / "I have finished."past perfect : He said he had seen it / she had finished.
will : "I will return."would : He said he would return.
can / may / mustcould / might / had to

Si le verbe introducteur est au présent, rien ne change : She says she is proud. Et si ce qui est rapporté reste vrai, la concordance est facultative : He said that art is a weapon.

Les repères de temps et de lieu

now → then, today → that day, yesterday → the day before, tomorrow → the next day / the following day, here → there, this → that, ago → before, last week → the week before.

Ordres et conseils rapportés

tell / ask / advise + sb + (not) to + BV : "Don't move!" → The photographer told them not to move.

Une question indirecte est une question insérée dans une phrase : I wonder…, Can you tell me…, I'd like to know…, She asked…. On la rencontre pour rapporter une question, mais aussi pour poser une question de manière plus polie.

L'ordre des mots : sujet + verbe

Dans une question indirecte, il n'y a pas d'inversion et pas d'auxiliaire do / does / did :

  • "Where is the painting?" → Can you tell me where the painting is?
  • "Why did he paint her?" → I wonder why he painted her.
  • "Who owns the bronzes?" → The question is who owns the bronzes. (who sujet : même ordre)

If / whether

Une question fermée (réponse oui / non) est introduite par if ou whether : "Is it a cartoon?" → She asked if (whether) it was a cartoon. On emploie whether devant or not et après une préposition : They discussed whether the objects should be returned.

La ponctuation

Après I wonder… ou She asked…, la phrase se termine par un point. Le point d'interrogation n'apparaît que si la phrase principale est une question : Do you know when it was painted?

Attention

Erreur fréquente : I wonder what does it mean. On écrit I wonder what it means. Rapportée au passé : He asked what it meant.

L'emphase avec do, does, did

Dans une phrase affirmative au présent simple ou au prétérit, on peut ajouter do / does / did (accentué à l'oral) devant la base verbale pour insister, contredire ou confirmer :

  • I do like his cartoons! (j'aime vraiment)
  • "Nobody listened to her." "That's not true, they did listen to her."
  • She does look powerful in this portrait.

Le verbe qui suit est à la base verbale : he did visit, jamais he did visited. À l'impératif, do rend une invitation plus chaleureuse : Do come in!

Les adverbes de degré

SensAdverbesExemple
très fortextremely, deeply, highly, incrediblyan extremely powerful image
totalement (avec un adjectif « absolu »)absolutely, totally, utterlyabsolutely terrifying, utterly ridiculous
certitudeundoubtedly, definitely, clearlyIt is undoubtedly his best work.
moyennementquite, rather, fairlya rather dark painting
à peine, presque pasbarely, hardly, scarcelyYou can barely see the ships.

Absolutely s'emploie avec des adjectifs extrêmes (absolutely amazing, absolutely furious), very avec des adjectifs ordinaires (very good) : on ne dit pas very amazing. Barely et hardly ont déjà un sens négatif : I could hardly believe it (et non couldn't hardly).

Les exclamatives

  • How + adjectif / adverbe (+ sujet + verbe) : How courageous they were! How beautifully she sings!
  • What + a / an + adjectif + nom dénombrable singulier : What an ordeal it must have been! What a striking picture!
  • What + (adjectif +) nom pluriel ou indénombrable, sans article : What bright colours! What courage!
  • so + adjectif, such (a) + (adjectif +) nom : The song was so moving! It was such a brave decision!
Attention

L'ordre des mots ne change pas après How ou What : How strange it is! (et non How strange is it!, qui serait une question).

Le Federal Art Project du New Deal fut une forme de mécénat public.
  • L'art résiste et témoigne : The Migration Series de Jacob Lawrence, Strange Fruit chanté par Billie Holiday (1939), The Problem We All Live With de Norman Rockwell (1964). La restitution des bronzes du Bénin pose la question de l'héritage colonial.

But is every discovery good for humanity and for the planet? Who decides what is acceptable? Dans ce chapitre, tu étudies la conquête spatiale, la transition énergétique en Écosse et la bioéthique, et tu apprends à formuler des hypothèses, à exprimer la probabilité et à articuler un argument.

sections.html:
L'espace a longtemps été le terrain de jeu des États. Aujourd'hui, des entreprises privées y envoient des fusées, des satellites et des touristes. Lis le texte et repère les règles qui existent et les questions qui restent ouvertes.

The province of all mankind

In 1967, during the Cold War, the United States, the Soviet Union and the United Kingdom signed the Outer Space Treaty, which more than 110 countries have now joined. It declares that space is "the province of all mankind": no country can claim the Moon or any other celestial body, and nuclear weapons cannot be placed in orbit. Two years later, in July 1969, the American astronauts of Apollo 11 planted a flag on the Moon, but the flag did not make the Moon American.

The new space race

In the 21st century, billionaire entrepreneurs have entered the race. Elon Musk's company SpaceX, founded in 2002, landed the first stage of a Falcon 9 rocket in December 2015: reusable rockets made launches much cheaper. In July 2021, Richard Branson and Jeff Bezos each flew to the edge of space aboard their own companies' spacecraft, and space tourism became a reality for the very rich.

The treaty says nothing clear about resources. In 2015, a US law allowed American companies to own the resources they extract from asteroids or the Moon, and in 2020 the United States launched the Artemis Accords, a set of non-binding principles for exploring the Moon, signed by dozens of countries. Critics fear that space-mining will benefit only a few rich nations and companies.

A space junkyard?

Thousands of satellites now orbit the Earth, and tens of thousands of pieces of space debris larger than ten centimetres are tracked. A single collision can create thousands of new fragments, which can in turn destroy other satellites. Some scientists warn that, if nothing is done, some orbits could become unusable.

sections.titre: Scotland: energy from coal to wind
sections.html:
L'Écosse a connu la révolution industrielle, le boom du pétrole, puis la course aux énergies renouvelables. Lis le texte et construis une frise des énergies écossaises.

Steam and coal

In 1769, the Scottish engineer James Watt patented an improved steam engine that used far less coal. His invention became a catalyst for the Industrial Revolution: factories, mines and later railways could use steam power. Coal from central Scotland fed the shipyards of the River Clyde, near Glasgow, which built some of the largest ships in the world.

Black gold

In 1970, oil was discovered in the Forties field, in the North Sea. Aberdeen became the "oil capital of Europe", and tens of thousands of jobs depended on the platforms. But fossil fuels emit greenhouse gases, and the oil will not last for ever. Scotland's last coal-fired power station, Longannet, closed in 2016.

The windy country

Scotland now produces most of its electricity from renewable sources, mainly wind. Whitelee, near Glasgow, is the largest onshore wind farm in the United Kingdom. In 2017, the world's first floating wind farm, Hywind Scotland, began operating off the coast of Peterhead. Seagreen, located about 27 km off the coast in the North Sea, is Scotland's largest offshore wind farm, with 114 turbines. The Scottish government aims to reach net zero emissions by 2045.

The transition has a cost. Some residents object to turbines that spoil the landscape, energy bills have soared in recent years, and oil workers want to be sure that new jobs will replace the old ones: this is called a "just transition".

Méthode : présenter un pour et un contre

On the one hand, wind power is clean and renewable. On the other hand, some people object to its impact on the landscape. All things considered, I think that…

sections.titre: The quest for the perfect human
sections.html:
Améliorer l'être humain : rêve de progrès ou cauchemar ? Lis le texte et repère, pour chaque époque, une avancée et une inquiétude.

A warning from fiction

In 1818, the English writer Mary Shelley published Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus. A young scientist, Victor Frankenstein, gives life to a creature made from parts of dead bodies, then abandons it in horror. The novel asks a question that is still relevant: is a scientist responsible for what he creates? In Brave New World (1932), Aldous Huxley imagined a society where babies are produced in laboratories and conditioned for their future role.

The dark history of eugenics

In 1883, the British scientist Francis Galton invented the word eugenics: the idea of "improving" the human race by controlling who could have children. In the early 20th century, many American states passed laws allowing the forced sterilisation of people considered "unfit", and in 1927 the Supreme Court approved such a law. Tens of thousands of people were sterilised against their will. Eugenics was later discredited, especially after Nazi crimes.

Science today

In 1996, scientists at the Roslin Institute, near Edinburgh, created Dolly the sheep, the first mammal cloned from an adult cell. In 2003, the Human Genome Project finished reading the human genetic code. Since then, gene therapy has made great progress: in 2023, the United Kingdom became the first country to approve a treatment based on the CRISPR gene-editing technique, for sickle cell disease.

New techniques raise ethical questions. In the UK, the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Authority can allow parents to select an embryo that will be a compatible donor for a sick brother or sister: a saviour sibling. Bioethicists ask where treatment ends and human enhancement begins. Should parents be able to choose the height, intelligence or eye colour of their children?

Human ou humane ?

Human = humain (qui concerne l'être humain : the human body) ; humane = humain au sens de bienveillant, qui évite la souffrance : a humane treatment.

La phrase conditionnelle relie une condition (proposition en if) et sa conséquence. Le temps employé dans la proposition en if indique si l'hypothèse est réelle, imaginaire ou passée.

TypeProposition en ifPrincipaleExemple

  • Jamais de will ni de would dans la proposition en if : If it rains tomorrow… (pas if it will rain).
  • Avec be, la langue soignée emploie were à toutes les personnes : If I were a scientist, I would study genes.
  • La virgule n'est nécessaire que si la proposition en if vient en premier.
  • could ou might peuvent remplacer would : If we built more turbines, we could close the last power stations.

Unless, as long as, provided that

unless = if… not (à moins que) : Unless we act now, some orbits will become unusable. = If we don't act now… Le verbe après unless est affirmatif.

as long as / provided (that) = à condition que : Space tourism is acceptable as long as it does not pollute. Ces conjonctions suivent les mêmes règles de temps que if.

Attention

If (si, condition) et whether (si, alternative dans une question indirecte) ne sont pas interchangeables dans une conditionnelle : I'll go if you go, mais I don't know whether he'll come.

sections.titre: Grammar: inversion and modals of probability
sections.html:
L'hypothèse par inversion

Dans une langue soutenue, on peut supprimer if et placer l'auxiliaire avant le sujet :

  • If she had known… → Had she known the risks, she would have refused.
  • If I were in charge… → Were I in charge, I would ban space tourism.
  • If you should need help… → Should you need help, contact the lab.

La négation se place après le sujet : Had Watt not improved the engine, … (jamais Hadn't Watt… dans cette structure).

Les modaux de probabilité

Ils expriment le degré de certitude de celui qui parle.

CertitudeSur le présent ou le futurSur le passé
quasi-certitudemust + BV : He must be a bioethicist.must have + participe passé : The debris must have hit the satellite.
possibilitémay / might / could + BV : Space-mining might become profitable.may / might / could have + participe passé : The engineers might have made a mistake.
impossibilitécan't / couldn't + BV : That can't be true.can't / couldn't have + participe passé : He can't have seen the launch: he was in London.
forte probabilité (futur)will probably / be likely to : Prices are likely to soar.was / were likely to

On peut aussi nuancer avec des adverbes : perhaps, maybe, probably, certainly, undoubtedly.

Attention

Le contraire de must (probabilité) est can't, pas mustn't : It can't be Dolly (ce ne peut pas être Dolly). Mustn't exprime une interdiction (chapitre 5).

Les connecteurs donnent sa logique à un argument. Repère leur sens et leur construction.

SensConnecteursExemple
additionmoreover, furthermore, besides, in addition, what's moreWind power is clean. Moreover, it creates jobs.
illustrationfor instance, for example, such as, likerenewable sources such as wind and tides
causebecause, since, as, because of + nom, due to + nomLaunches are cheaper because of reusable rockets.
conséquenceso, therefore, consequently, as a result, thusOil will run out; therefore, we must invest in wind.
oppositionbut, however, whereas, while, on the contrary, on the one hand… on the other handCoal pollutes, whereas wind is clean.
concessionalthough, even though, though, yet, despite / in spite of + nom ou V-ing, neverthelessAlthough the treaty exists, the rules on space-mining are unclear.
conclusionto sum up, all in all, all things considered, in conclusionAll things considered, the benefits outweigh the risks.

Construction

  • although, even though, whereas, because + sujet + verbe : Although it is expensive, gene therapy saves lives.
  • despite, in spite of, because of, due to + nom ou V-ing : Despite the cost, the project went ahead. In spite of being expensive, …
  • however, moreover, therefore, nevertheless en tête de phrase, suivis d'une virgule : However, critics disagree.
Attention

Despite ne prend jamais of : despite the risks (ou in spite of the risks). Et even if (même si, hypothèse) n'a pas le sens de even though (bien que, fait réel).

sections.html:
Le parc national est une invention américaine, reprise dans le monde entier. Lis le texte et repère les dates clés, puis les tensions entre protection et fréquentation.

The first national park

On 1 March 1872, President Ulysses S. Grant signed a law creating Yellowstone National Park, in the American West: it was the first national park in the world. Its geysers, hot springs and wildlife were to be preserved "for the benefit and enjoyment of the people". In 1916, the US government created the National Park Service to manage the growing number of parks.

John Muir, the wilderness prophet

John Muir, born in Scotland in 1838, emigrated to the United States as a child. He fell in love with the Sierra Nevada mountains of California and spent his life defending them. Thanks partly to his articles, Yosemite became a national park in 1890, and in 1892 he founded the Sierra Club, one of the first environmental organisations. In 1903, he went camping in Yosemite with President Theodore Roosevelt, who later protected millions of acres of public land.

Across the English-speaking world

Canada created its first national park at Banff, in the Rocky Mountains, in 1885. In Britain, the fight was about access: in 1932, hundreds of walkers took part in a "mass trespass" on Kinder Scout to demand the right to walk on private moorland. The Peak District became the first British national park in 1951.

Paradise lost?

National parks also have a darker side. Many were created on land where Native peoples had lived for thousands of years, and these peoples were forced to leave. Today, millions of visitors every year cause traffic jams, pollution and erosion. Rangers ask visitors to follow the "Leave No Trace" principles: you must take your rubbish home, you mustn't feed the animals, and you have to stay on the trails.

Sécheresses, ouragans, incendies : face aux événements extrêmes, les sociétés révèlent leurs fragilités et leurs capacités d'adaptation. Lis le texte et repère, pour chaque catastrophe, une cause humaine et une réponse.

The Dust Bowl

In the 1930s, the southern Great Plains of the United States were hit by years of drought. Farmers had ploughed up the native grasses that held the soil in place, so the wind blew the dry earth away in gigantic dust storms. On "Black Sunday", 14 April 1935, a black cloud turned day into night. Hundreds of thousands of people left the region, many of them for California. John Steinbeck told their story in The Grapes of Wrath (1939), and the government created a service to teach farmers how to protect the soil.

Hurricane Katrina

On 29 August 2005, Hurricane Katrina hit the coast of Louisiana and Mississippi. In New Orleans, the levees that protected the city broke and about 80 % of the city was flooded. More than 1,800 people died. The slow response of the authorities was strongly criticised, especially because the poorest neighbourhoods, often Black neighbourhoods, suffered most. The city later rebuilt and strengthened its flood defences.

Australia's Black Summer

During the summer of 2019-2020, huge bushfires burned millions of hectares of forest in south-eastern Australia. According to a WWF study, nearly three billion animals were killed or displaced. Scientists explained that climate change makes such fires more frequent and more intense. Since then, Australians have been learning to live with fire: early warnings, fire bans and the revival of Aboriginal "cool burning", a traditional practice of small controlled fires that reduces fuel on the ground.

Méthode : exprimer des sentiments

I was appalled by… / I find it heartbreaking that… / It is shocking that… / I can't help feeling sorry for… / What strikes me is…

sections.titre: Sacred nature in art and fiction
sections.html:
Pour certains artistes et certains peuples, la nature n'est pas seulement belle : elle est sacrée. Lis le texte et repère comment chaque œuvre ou chaque décision exprime ce lien.

The Romantic poets

At the beginning of the 19th century, English Romantic poets turned to nature as a source of emotion and spiritual truth. In I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud (1807), William Wordsworth describes a host of golden daffodils beside a lake in the Lake District; long afterwards, the memory of the flowers still fills his heart with pleasure. For the Romantics, nature could heal the soul.

Walden

In 1845, the American writer Henry David Thoreau built a small cabin in the woods near Walden Pond, in Massachusetts, and lived there for about two years. In Walden (1854), he explains that he wanted to live simply and "deliberately", far from the noise of modern society. His book inspired generations of environmentalists.

Painting the wilderness

From the 1820s, a group of American painters known as the Hudson River School, led by Thomas Cole, painted vast landscapes of mountains, rivers and forests. Their wilderness looks grand and almost divine, a kind of natural cathedral. A century later, the photographer Ansel Adams captured Yosemite in black and white, and his pictures helped to defend the parks.

A river with rights

For the Māori people of New Zealand, nature is linked to their ancestors. For the Whanganui iwi (tribe), the Whanganui River is an ancestor: "I am the river, and the river is me," says a traditional saying. In 2017, after a struggle of more than a century, New Zealand's Parliament recognised the river as a legal person, with its own rights and two guardians to speak for it.

Weather and disasters

EnglishFrançaisExample
a droughtune sécheresseThe drought lasted for years.
a flood / to floodune inondation / inonder80 % of the city was flooded.
a leveeune digue (le long d'un fleuve)The levees broke.

to evacuate / evacueesévacuer / les personnes évacuéesThousands were evacuated.
to adapt tos'adapter àWe must adapt to climate change.
to alleviatesoulager, atténuerAid alleviated the suffering.
harshrude, rigoureuxa harsh climate
Prononciation

Les consonnes affriquées /ʧ/ et /ʤ/ : change, nature, future /ˈfjuːʧə/ ; jungle, energy, damage /ˈdæmɪʤ/. Lettre muette : le l de calm, walk, half ; le w de wreck, wrong.

L'obligation

  • must + BV : obligation imposée par celui qui parle, ou règle écrite : You must stay on the trails.
  • have to + BV : obligation extérieure (règlement, circonstances) ; se conjugue à tous les temps : Visitors have to buy a pass. In 2005, thousands of people had to leave their homes. You will have to wait.
  • should / ought to + BV : conseil, devoir moral : We should protect wetlands. We ought to respect the land.
  • had better + BV : conseil pressant (sinon…) : You'd better take water with you.
  • shall : dans les textes juridiques, obligation : Visitors shall not enter this area. ; dans une question, une proposition : Shall we go?

Interdiction ou absence d'obligation ?

FormeSensExemple
mustn't + BVinterdiction (il ne faut pas)You mustn't feed the bears.
don't have to / needn't + BVabsence d'obligation (ce n'est pas la peine)You don't have to pay: entry is free.
be not allowed to / can'tinterdiction (pas le droit)You are not allowed to camp here.

La permission

can / may (plus formel) / be allowed to (à tous les temps) : You can fish in this lake. May I take a photo? In the 1930s, walkers were not allowed to cross private moorland. Demander poliment : Could I…? Would you mind if I opened the window?

La capacité

can (présent), could (passé, capacité générale), be able to (tous les temps, et réussite ponctuelle dans le passé) : Bears can run fast. After the flood, they were able to rebuild. One day we will be able to predict fires better.

Attention

Les modaux (must, can, should) n'ont ni -s, ni to après eux, ni futur : he must go, you will have to go (et non will must). « J'ai dû partir » se dit I had to leave.

Faire faire : make, let, have, get

StructureSensExemple
make + sb + BVobliger, faire faire (contrainte ou effet)The storm made the farmers leave. His death made me cry.
let + sb + BVlaisser, permettreThe rangers let us camp near the lake.
have + sb + BVfaire faire (service, demande)The park had volunteers plant trees.
get + sb + to + BVconvaincre qqn de faireMuir got the president to protect the land.
have / get + objet + participe passéfaire faire qqch par qqn (on ne dit pas qui)They had their house rebuilt. She got her roof repaired.

Au passif, make prend to : The farmers were made to leave. Let n'a pas de passif : on emploie be allowed to.

Les structures résultatives

L'anglais peut exprimer en une seule proposition une action et son résultat : verbe + complément + adjectif ou particule de résultat.

  • He watered the roses flat. (il a arrosé les roses, si bien qu'elles se sont couchées)
  • The wind blew the door open. (le vent a ouvert la porte en soufflant)
  • The fire burned the forest down. (l'incendie a réduit la forêt en cendres)
  • She painted the cabin green.

Le français traduit souvent le résultat par le verbe et la manière par un complément : He kicked the door open = il a ouvert la porte d'un coup de pied.

sections.titre: Grammar: phrasal verbs and the gerund
sections.html:
Les phrasal verbs

Un phrasal verb associe un verbe et une particule (up, down, out, off, away…) ; le sens n'est pas toujours la somme des deux.

Phrasal verbSensExemple
set upcréer, fonderMuir set up the Sierra Club.
cut downabattre (des arbres) ; réduireThey cut down the forest. Cut down on plastic!
run out ofmanquer de, être à court deThe farmers ran out of water.
wipe outanéantir, rayer de la carteThe fires wiped out entire species.
put outéteindre (un feu)Firefighters put out the fire.
look afters'occuper deRangers look after the park.
give upabandonner, renoncer àMany farmers gave up their land.
carry oncontinuerCarry on walking until the lake.
figure outcomprendre, trouverScientists are trying to figure out why.
throw awayjeterDon't throw away your rubbish here.

Avec un complément pronom, la particule se place après le pronom : They put it out (et non put out it). Avec un nom, les deux ordres sont possibles : put out the fire / put the fire out.

Un pronom réfléchi peut s'insérer : She pulled herself together (elle s'est ressaisie). They looked after themselves in the wild.

Le gérondif (V-ing)

  • sujet : Protecting wildlife is everyone's business.
  • après certains verbes : enjoy, avoid, stop, keep, mind, can't stand, finish, suggest : We enjoyed hiking. Avoid feeding the animals.
  • après une préposition : before leaving, without making noise, interested in protecting, et après look forward to : I'm looking forward to visiting Banff.
Attention

Stop doing = arrêter de faire ; stop to do = s'arrêter pour faire. Remember doing = se souvenir d'avoir fait ; remember to do = penser à faire.

• Yellowstone (1872) est le premier parc national du monde ; John Muir a défendu Yosemite et fondé le Sierra Club (1892) ; Banff (1885) et le Peak District (1951) ont suivi. Les parcs ont aussi chassé des peuples autochtones et souffrent de la surfréquentation.
  • Face aux extrêmes : le Dust Bowl des années 1930 (The Grapes of Wrath), l'ouragan Katrina (2005) à La Nouvelle-Orléans, le Black Summer australien (2019-2020) ; les sociétés s'adaptent (digues, alertes, brûlages traditionnels).
  • La nature sacralisée : Wordsworth et les romantiques, Walden de Thoreau, la Hudson River School ; en 2017, le fleuve Whanganui est devenu une personne juridique.
  • must / have to : obligation ; mustn't : interdiction ; don't have to : absence d'obligation ; be allowed to : permission ; be able to : capacité à tous les temps.
  • make / let / have + sb + BV ; get sb to + BV ; have sth done ; résultatives : The wind blew the door open.
  • Phrasal verbs : set up, cut down, run out of, wipe out, put out, look after ; pronom avant la particule (put it out). Gérondif : sujet, après enjoy, avoid et après une préposition (look forward to + V-ing).

Music, money, tourists and migrants travel in every direction, but not always on equal terms. sections.html:
Les Caraïbes anglophones sont petites par la taille, mais immenses par leur influence. Lis le texte et repère ce que la région a reçu du monde, et ce qu'elle lui a donné.

From colonies to nations

For centuries, the islands of the Caribbean were European colonies where enslaved Africans were forced to work on sugar plantations. After the abolition of slavery in the British Empire in the 1830s, workers also came from India and China. In the 20th century, the British colonies became independent: Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago in 1962, Barbados in 1966. In 2021, Barbados went further and became a republic, replacing the British monarch with its own president.

In 1973, several of these countries founded the Caribbean Community, CARICOM, to cooperate on trade, education and health. Today it has fifteen full members.

A small region, a big voice

Caribbean culture travels far. Reggae, born in Jamaica in the late 1960s and made famous by Bob Marley, was added to UNESCO's list of the intangible cultural heritage of humanity in 2018. The steelpan and calypso come from Trinidad, whose carnival inspired carnivals in London, Toronto and New York. The poet Derek Walcott, born on the island of Saint Lucia in 1930, received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1992; in his long poem Omeros, he retells Homer's epic with Caribbean fishermen.

Unequal exchanges

The exchanges are not always equal. Many economies depend on tourism, especially on cruise ships from North America, and much of the money leaves the islands again. Hurricanes regularly destroy homes and roads. Many young graduates leave for the United States, Canada or Britain, and the Jamaican diaspora is now very large. Their families at home often depend on the money they send back.

Définition

Une diaspora est l'ensemble des membres d'un peuple dispersés hors de leur pays d'origine. Les envois d'argent des émigrés à leur famille s'appellent les remittances.

Porto Rico appartient aux États-Unis sans en être un État. Lis le texte et repère les étapes de cette relation, puis les trois options en débat.

An American territory

Puerto Rico, an island in the Caribbean, was a Spanish colony for four centuries. In 1898, after the Spanish-American War, Spain ceded it to the United States. In 1917, the Jones Act made Puerto Ricans US citizens. Since 1952, the island has been a Commonwealth (in Spanish, Estado Libre Asociado): it has its own constitution and governor, but it remains under the authority of the US Congress.

Citizens, but not quite

About 3.2 million people live on the island. Puerto Ricans can travel and work freely in the fifty states, and they serve in the US army. However, as long as they live on the island, they cannot vote in presidential elections, and they are represented in Congress by a single Resident Commissioner who cannot vote on final laws. Spanish and English are both official languages, but Spanish is the language of daily life for most people.

Three possible futures

Puerto Ricans are divided. Some want the island to become the 51st state of the United States, with full rights. Others prefer to keep the current status, which protects their Spanish-speaking identity. A minority want independence. In several non-binding referendums, most recently in 2020 and 2024, a majority of voters chose statehood, but only the US Congress can admit a new state, and it has never done so.

In September 2017, Hurricane Maria devastated the island and left most residents without electricity for months. The official death toll was later estimated at about 3,000. Many Puerto Ricans felt that they had been treated like second-class citizens, and tens of thousands left for the mainland: today more Puerto Ricans live in the fifty states than on the island.

sections.titre: Vancouver and Seattle: two cities, one region
sections.html:
Deux villes séparées par une frontière, mais unies par une même région : lis le texte et compare Vancouver et Seattle point par point (histoire, économie, culture).

Cascadia

Vancouver, in the Canadian province of British Columbia, and Seattle, in the US state of Washington, are only about 200 kilometres apart. Both stand on the Pacific coast, between the ocean and the mountains, in a green and rainy region that some people call Cascadia. Both were built on the lands of the Coast Salish peoples; Seattle is even named after a Duwamish and Suquamish chief, Si'ahl.

Two cities, two stories

Vancouver became a city in 1886, when the Canadian Pacific Railway arrived, and was named after the British navigator George Vancouver. Today it is Canada's largest port and one of the most multicultural cities in the country, with large Chinese and South Asian communities. It hosted the Expo 86 world's fair and the 2010 Winter Olympics, and its film industry has earned it the nickname "Hollywood North".

Seattle grew with the timber trade and the Klondike gold rush of the 1890s. Its symbol, the Space Needle, was built for the 1962 World's Fair. The city is the birthplace of Boeing (1916) and the home of Amazon and Starbucks, while Microsoft is based nearby. In the 1990s, it gave the world grunge music.

Cooperation and rivalry

Every day, workers, students and tourists cross the border at the Peace Arch, a monument built in 1921 to celebrate friendship between the two countries. The two cities cooperate on technology and research, and both hosted matches of the 2026 FIFA World Cup. But they are also rivals: their football teams, the Whitecaps and the Sounders, compete every year for the Cascadia Cup. And the American pull is strong: many Canadian tech workers are attracted by higher salaries in Seattle, while some Americans move north for a calmer life.

Méthode : comparer deux villes

Both cities are… / Neither city is… / Vancouver is bigger than…, whereas Seattle… / Like Vancouver, Seattle… / Unlike Seattle, Vancouver…

sections.titre: Grammar: compound adjectives, noun groups, distributives
sections.html:
Les adjectifs composés

On les forme avec un trait d'union. Ils se placent devant le nom et restent invariables : le nom qu'ils contiennent ne prend pas de -s.

  • nombre + nom : a ten-minute break, a 200-kilometre journey, a three-year-old girl, a four-hour flight (et non a ten-minutes break)
  • adjectif + nom + -ed : a black-haired man, a blue-eyed child, a warm-hearted host
  • adjectif / adverbe + participe : a well-known poet, a fast-growing city, a Spanish-speaking island, a hand-made quilt

Compare : The flight lasts four hours. / It is a four-hour flight.

Le groupe nominal complexe

StructureEmploiExemples
N N (nom composé)catégorie, matière, fonction ; le 2e nom est le noyaua football team, a gold rush, a wind farm, a teacup
N's N (cas possessif)possession par une personne, un groupe, un lieu ; duréeCanada's largest port, a children's book, a day's work
N of Npartie, quantité, contenanta cup of tea, the end of the war, a pair of shoes

Dans un nom composé, le premier nom est au singulier : a ticket office (pas a tickets office).

Les distributifs

MotSensExemple
both (+ pluriel)les deuxBoth cities are on the Pacific coast.
either (+ singulier)l'un ou l'autre (de deux)You can take either road.
neither (+ singulier)aucun des deuxNeither city is a capital.
each (+ singulier)chaque, pris un par un (deux ou plus)Each island has its own carnival.
every (+ singulier)chaque, tous sans exception (trois ou plus)Every state has two senators.

Avec un pronom ou un déterminant : both of them, either of them, neither of us, each of the islands. Structures corrélatives : both… and, either… or, neither… nor : Neither Seattle nor Vancouver is a capital.

Wish et if only expriment un souhait irréalisable ou un regret. Le temps du verbe qui suit est décalé dans le passé.

Ce que l'on regretteStructureExemple
une situation présentewish + prétérit (were pour be)I wish I lived in Vancouver. (je n'y vis pas) / I wish I were taller.
un fait passéwish + past perfectI wish I had visited Jamaica. (je ne l'ai pas fait)
le comportement de quelqu'un (agacement, souhait de changement)wish + sb + would + BVI wish the media would talk more about Puerto Rico.
une capacitéwish + could + BVThey wish they could vote for the president.

If only a le même sens, en plus fort : If only they had listened! If only I had more time!

Préférences : would rather

  • I'd rather (would rather) + BV : je préférerais : I'd rather stay in Seattle.
  • I'd rather + sujet + prétérit : je préférerais que quelqu'un… : I'd rather you came with us.
Attention

Pour un souhait réalisable, on n'emploie pas wish mais hope : I hope you have a good trip (et non I wish you have). Mais on dit I wish you a good trip (nom complément) et I wish to + BV dans une langue soutenue (= I want to).

sections.html:
Les questions en How

QuestionPorte surExemple
How often…?la fréquenceHow often do ferries leave? Every hour.
How many times…?le nombre de foisHow many times have you been there? Twice.
How long…?la durée ; la longueurHow long does the trip take? About three hours.
How far…?la distanceHow far is Seattle from Vancouver? About 200 km.
How much / How many…?la quantité (indénombrable / dénombrable), le prixHow much does a ticket cost? How many people live there?
How tall / high / wide / deep / old…?la mesure, l'âgeHow tall is the Space Needle? How old is the city?
How well…?le degré, la qualitéHow well do you speak Spanish?

Les question tags

Un tag est une petite question en fin de phrase (« n'est-ce pas ? »). On reprend l'auxiliaire de la phrase et le pronom sujet, en inversant la polarité :

  • phrase affirmative → tag négatif : Puerto Rico is a US territory, isn't it? You have been to Kingston, haven't you?
  • phrase négative → tag affirmatif : Barbados isn't a monarchy any more, is it? She can't vote, can she?
  • sans auxiliaire, on emploie do / does / did : Walcott won the Nobel Prize, didn't he? You live in Seattle, don't you?
  • cas particuliers : I am right, aren't I? Let's go, shall we? Close the door, will you?

Intonation descendante : on attend une confirmation ; montante : on pose vraiment la question.

Les réponses courtes

On répond avec le sujet pronom et l'auxiliaire, sans répéter le verbe : "Is Seattle in Canada?" "No, it isn't." "Did you see the Space Needle?" "Yes, I did." "Have they ever been to Trinidad?" "Yes, they have." Pour réagir : "I love reggae." "So do I." / "I don't like the rain." "Neither do I." / "He's never been there." "Hasn't he?"

• Les Caraïbes anglophones sont devenues indépendantes à partir de 1962 (la Barbade est une république depuis 2021) et coopèrent dans la CARICOM (1973). Leur culture rayonne (reggae, calypso, carnavals, Derek Walcott, prix Nobel 1992), mais les échanges restent inégaux (tourisme, ouragans, fuite des cerveaux).
  • Porto Rico, cédé aux États-Unis en 1898, est un Commonwealth depuis 1952 ; ses habitants sont citoyens américains depuis 1917, mais ne votent pas à l'élection présidentielle sur l'île. Le débat oppose statut actuel, 51e État et indépendance ; seul le Congrès peut admettre un nouvel État.
  • Vancouver et Seattle, à environ 200 km l'une de l'autre, forment la région de Cascadia : coopération (Peace Arch, technologie) et rivalité, avec l'attraction des salaires américains.
  • Adjectifs composés invariables (a ten-minute break) ; noms composés (a wind farm), cas possessif (Canada's largest port), N of N ; both + pluriel, either / neither / each / every + singulier.
  • wish + prétérit (regret présent), + past perfect (regret passé), + would (souhait de changement) ; if only ; I'd rather.
  • Questions en How (often, long, far, much, many, tall) ; tags : auxiliaire + pronom, polarité inversée (isn't it?, didn't he?) ; réponses courtes (Yes, I did. So do I.).
